title: About CIA Part 3
description: What CIA Part 3 looks like, who sits it, how to read its questions as the chief audit executive running the function, how to pace and prepare, how to book it, and how passing fits into becoming certified. Written in plain language by KaiSip from The IIA's published information.
disclaimer: Certified Internal Auditor® and CIA® are registered trademarks, and Global Internal Audit Standards™ is a trademark, of The IIA (The Institute of Internal Auditors, Inc.). KaiSip is an independent study aid. It is not affiliated with, sponsored, endorsed or licensed by The IIA. All notes and questions are written by KaiSip; none are actual exam questions. The IIA alone sets the exam rules and decides eligibility and certification. No study app can promise a pass, including this one.
check_before_booking: Fees, dates, languages and rules on this page were checked on the date shown. They can change, so check theiia.org before you book.

sections.title: The exam at a glance
sections.summary: CIA Part 3, Internal Audit Function, is 100 multiple-choice questions in 120 minutes, taken on a computer at a Pearson VUE test center. A scaled score of 600 or higher passes.
items: 100 multiple-choice questions in 120 minutes: 1.2 minutes, or 72 seconds, a question on average.
The IIA's published sample questions each have four options, A to D. KaiSip's practice questions use the same shape, with one best answer.
Part 3 is one of the three CIA exam parts. It is about the internal audit function as a whole: running it, planning its work, showing its quality, and reporting and following up engagement results.
Planning one engagement, gathering its evidence and supervising the work in progress belong to Part 2, Internal Audit Engagement. Part 3 picks up when results are reported and monitored.
Scores are reported on a scale from 250 to 750, and 600 or higher passes. 600 is a point on that scale, not a percent of the questions.
Wrong answers are not penalized, so answer every question, including the ones you are unsure of.
No breaks are scheduled. You may step away, but the clock keeps running.
You sit the exam in person at a Pearson VUE test center. The IIA ended online testing on 27 May 2025.
The exam is non-disclosed: The IIA does not publish current questions and answers. Every KaiSip question is written by KaiSip, and none is a real exam question.
Part 3 rests on the Global Internal Audit Standards, published on 9 January 2024 and effective from 9 January 2025.

sections.title: What Part 3 is and who sits it
sections.summary: Part 3 is for candidates on the three-part CIA route. You can sit it before your work experience is complete, and in any order with the other two parts.
items: Entry to the three-part CIA route: a degree, or an active Internal Audit Practitioner (IAP) designation. You may sit the exams before your internal audit experience is complete; the experience is needed to be certified, not to test.
An active IAP holder gets a waiver for Part 1, the exam they already passed as the IAP exam, and sits Parts 2 and 3 only.

The IIA does not prescribe an order for the three parts. KaiSip's view: Part 3 takes Part 1's rules and Part 2's engagement up to the whole function, so it usually reads more easily once the other two are familiar.

Your seat in Part 3: the chief audit executive running the function. You propose, manage, report and escalate; the board approves and oversees; senior management gives input and support; management owns risks and actions.
Some Section D questions put you beside the internal auditors who draft results and follow up actions. The chief audit executive still approves what is issued and decides what is escalated.
The CIA program must be completed within 3 years of approval.

sections.title: The four sections and their weights
sections.summary: The IIA's syllabus splits Part 3 into four sections. A section's weight is its share of the exam, so it is a fair guide to where your study time goes.

domains.name: Quality of the Internal Audit Function

items: Section D, Engagement Results and Monitoring, is the largest at 45%: the final communication, recommendations and action plans, residual risk, risk that management accepts, and following up and escalating actions.

Section A, Internal Audit Operations, is 25%: outside providers, the budget, people and technology, the function's strategy, and how the chief audit executive reports to the board and senior management.
Section B, Internal Audit Plan, is 15%: the audit universe, the organizationwide risk assessment, a plan that changes with the risks, and coordination with other assurance providers.
Section C, Quality of the Internal Audit Function, is 15%: the quality assurance and improvement program, disclosing nonconformance, and measuring the function's performance.
Sections D and A together are 70% of the exam, so most of your review time goes there.
The syllabus lists 18 numbered topics: 4 in Section A, 3 in B, 3 in C and 8 in D. KaiSip's notes use matching codes, so 3D6 is Part 3, Section D, topic 6.

sections.title: What the syllabus verbs tell you
sections.summary: The syllabus gives no depth label for a topic. Each topic line starts with a verb, and that verb signals how deep its questions can go. The three groups below are KaiSip's reading.
items: Know and explain (Describe, Recognize, Identify): 16 of Part 3's 18 topics. Expect to pick the right rule, role or step, often inside a short scenario about the function.
Use it (Demonstrate): 1 topic, writing the final engagement communication. Expect a draft or a situation and the question of what it needs.
Weigh and decide (Determine): 1 topic, recommendations and management action plans. Expect several reasonable actions and one that best reaches the cause at a fair cost.
A topic's detail lines often go deeper than its verb, so a know-and-explain topic still brings scenarios. Learn who approves, who is told and when well enough to spot them in a story.
Part 3's hard questions are rarely about a definition. They turn on the actor and the strength of the rule, so practice until you can say why the closest wrong choice loses.

sections.title: Syllabus, languages and Topical Requirements
sections.summary: KaiSip teaches the current syllabus and the 2024 Standards. Two languages were still on the older syllabus when this page was checked, so confirm which one your exam date uses.
items: The current syllabus was live in English by July 2025. Older books and many free notes still teach the earlier exam and its vocabulary; KaiSip does not.

The three-part exam is offered in 15 languages: English; Arabic; Simplified and Traditional Chinese; French, German, Polish, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish and Turkish; Japanese, Korean, Thai and Vietnamese.
Caution for Arabic: candidates sit the older 2019 syllabus through 27 December 2026 and move to the current one on 28 December 2026.
Caution for Simplified Chinese (mainland China only): it was still on the older 2019 syllabus when checked, and it moves to the current one during the December 2026 testing window.
If either caution applies to you, confirm with The IIA which syllabus your exam date uses before you rely on this course.

Two Part 3 topics, 3B1 and 3C1, ask you to recognize where Topical Requirements apply: in the plan, when a topic is planned, arises in an engagement or is requested, and in quality assessments, which check conformance with them.
Topical Requirements enter the exam on dates. Scored questions on a new one do not appear until at least 6 months after it takes effect.

Cybersecurity is testable now. When checked, The IIA's exam reference list also named Third-Party from March 2027, Organizational Behavior from June 2027 and Organizational Resilience from October 2027. The reference list sets which ones the exam tests.
A fifth, Anti-Corruption, was issued on 23 November 2026 and takes effect on 23 November 2027. No exam month was published for it when checked.

sections.title: Read each question as the chief audit executive
sections.summary: A short routine for every question: find what is asked, whether it concerns the function or one engagement, who acts, and how strong the rule is, then eliminate and choose. These are KaiSip's habits, built on the Standards.
steps: Read the last line first. Note what is asked for: an action, a person, a document, a report or a reason.

Place the question: the whole function (strategy, plan, budget, people, quality) or an engagement's results and follow-up? An option from one engagement's fieldwork is often Part 2's answer, not Part 3's.
Find the actor: the chief audit executive, the internal auditors, the board, senior management, the management responsible for the area, or an outside provider or assessor.
Find the priority word, such as FIRST, BEST or MOST, and check the strength: does the question ask what is required (a must) or what is good practice (a should)?
Rule out the options topic knowledge eliminates, often two. Settle the last two by asking who approves, who must be told and when, and who owns the action.
Say in one sentence why your choice beats the closest wrong choice. Then answer and move on.
items: The seat in one line: the chief audit executive proposes, manages, reports and escalates. The board approves and oversees; senior management gives input and support; management owns the risks, the controls and the actions.

"Get board approval" is right only where a Standard asks for it. The board approves the charter, the plan and its significant changes, the budget, the resource plan, the performance objectives and the external assessment plan. The strategy is reviewed, not approved.

"Tell the board promptly" is not always the answer. Accepted risk goes to the responsible management and senior management before the board; failed coordination goes to senior management first. Read whom the Standard names, and in what order.

A should is not a must. Meeting the board privately each year, adding a conformance statement and first raising accepted risk with the responsible management are shoulds. When the question asks what is required, a should loses.

Not the IT specialist, not the external auditor, not the risk owner, not the manager. Configuring a system, giving an opinion on the financial statements, choosing the risk response and fixing the problem are other people's jobs.
PRIMARY asks for the main purpose, MOST LIKELY for probability and not severity, and LEAST flips the test. The full list of priority words is on the final review week's cheat sheet.

sections.title: Who approves, who is told, and when
sections.summary: Many Part 3 questions turn on one of three things: who approves, who must be told, and how soon. These are KaiSip's patterns, built on the Standards for governing and managing the function and communicating results.
items: Charter: the chief audit executive develops it and discusses it with the board and senior management; the board approves it (Standard 6.2).

Plan: based on a documented risk assessment, done at least yearly with input from the board and senior management. The chief audit executive discusses the plan and significant changes with both; the board approves them (Standard 9.4).
An urgent plan change before the board can meet: inform the board at once and get formal approval as soon as possible. The Standards word this as a should.

Plan gaps: resource limits on coverage, a high-risk area left without assurance, conflicting demands, and scope or access limits are communicated timely to the board and senior management (Standard 9.4). Here telling is the must, not approval.

Budget: the chief audit executive develops it and seeks the board's approval. When money falls short, the impact goes promptly to the board and senior management (Standard 10.1). Never trim the plan quietly.
Strategy: a vision, strategic objectives and supporting initiatives, reviewed periodically with the board and senior management (Standard 9.2). No Standard asks the board to approve it.
Independence: the chief audit executive confirms the function's organizational independence to the board at least yearly, including any impairment and its safeguards (Standard 7.1).

Quality: internal assessment results go to the board and senior management at least yearly, external results when completed (Standard 8.3). The board approves the external assessment plan and receives the complete results directly from the assessor (Standard 8.4).

Coordination with other assurance providers: when it fails, the chief audit executive takes the concern to senior management first, and to the board only if needed. Relying on their work means documenting the basis; internal audit's conclusions stay the chief audit executive's (Standard 9.5).

Final communication: internal auditors draft it; the chief audit executive reviews and approves it before issue and decides who receives it (Standards 11.3, 15.1). A significant error is corrected promptly for everyone who received the original (Standard 11.4).

Accepted risk above appetite or tolerance: raise it first with the responsible management (a should), discuss it with senior management (a must), and escalate to the board if unresolved (a must). The chief audit executive never resolves the risk (Standard 11.5).

Follow-up: internal auditors confirm actions by inquiry, risk-based assessment and tracking, scaled to significance. A missed date: document management's explanation and discuss it with the chief audit executive, who judges whether delay means accepted risk (Standard 15.2).

sections.title: Common traps by section
sections.summary: Each section has a few traps that catch prepared candidates. Most send a matter to the wrong person, ask for an approval no Standard requires, or call a should a must. These are KaiSip's patterns, organized by The IIA's sections.
items: Operations: treating outsourced work as the provider's responsibility. Contracted auditors follow the Standards, the chief audit executive supervises their engagements, and the board still approves an adequate budget.
Operations: cutting engagements quietly when money runs short. The chief audit executive promptly reports the impact of insufficient resources to the board and senior management.

Operations: seeking the board's approval of the internal audit strategy, or a mission statement, as if a Standard required it. The strategy is reviewed with the board and senior management; the plan is what the board approves.

Plan: treating a senior manager's request as an order, or an audit cycle as a risk ranking. Requests and cycles are inputs; the documented risk assessment decides, and conflicting demands go to the board and senior management.

Plan: relying on another assurance provider because of its reputation. The work is evaluated first, the basis for reliance is documented, and the chief audit executive stays responsible for internal audit's conclusions.

Quality: claiming conformance with the Standards without support, or keeping a nonconformance quiet. A conformance statement needs the support of supervision and the quality program; a nonconformance is disclosed with its impact.

Quality: choosing an external assessor with no active Certified Internal Auditor on the team, or letting results reach the board only through the chief audit executive. The board receives them directly from the assessor.
Results: deleting a finding management fixed before the report went out. The action is acknowledged in the final communication, and the finding stays.
Results: softening a conclusion because management disagrees. Discuss the evidence, record both positions, and change a result only for a valid reason.
Monitoring: telling the board first when management accepts too much risk. The route runs through the responsible management and senior management, and only what stays unresolved reaches the board.
Monitoring: closing an action because its date has passed, or having internal audit implement it. Management implements; internal audit confirms, and a past-due action stays past due until confirmed.

sections.title: Pacing your 120 minutes
sections.summary: 120 minutes for 100 questions is 1.2 minutes each. Use that number to set two checkpoints, not to time every question.
items: Checkpoints: reach question 50 by minute 60; reach question 75 by minute 90. Look at the clock at those two points and otherwise leave it alone.
Ahead at a checkpoint? The minutes you have saved are your review time. Behind? Decide a little faster on the next few questions instead of rushing all of them.
If a question stalls you, choose your best answer and move on. Wrong answers are not penalized, so a best guess beats a blank.
No breaks are scheduled, and the clock keeps running if you take one. Plan as if you will sit straight through.

Part 3 mixes short rule questions with longer scenarios about the function. A long scenario takes more than the average and a plain rule question takes less, so judge your pace at the checkpoints, never on one question.

sections.title: Your score and KaiSip's numbers
sections.summary: The IIA reports a scaled score. KaiSip never shows one: it shows the percent you got right, by section, and its own readiness band. The two are different things.
items: The IIA converts your raw score to a reporting scale that runs from 250 to 750. A scaled score of 600 or higher passes.
600 is a point on that scale, not a percent of the questions. KaiSip knows of no published way to turn a percent correct into a scaled score, and it does not try.
If you pass, your score report shows no number at all. If you do not, it shows your score and the syllabus areas that need improvement.
A KaiSip mock result shows your percent correct for each section and your pace against the checkpoints. It is labeled as KaiSip's, and it is not The IIA's score.
KaiSip's readiness band is its own summary of your practice. It is a study signal, not a prediction of your result.
A good use of a practice percent: compare your four sections with each other and with last week, and give time to the section furthest behind its weight.

sections.title: Your last week before the exam
sections.summary: A calm seven-day plan with nothing new in it: one full timed mock early, then your slips, the section sheets and the close pairs, and rest at the end.
steps: Seven days out: sit one full timed mock of 100 questions in 120 minutes, using the two checkpoints. This is your last full mock before the exam.
Six days out: review each miss and name the thinking slip behind it. Then recall Section D, the largest section, and the route for accepted risk. Stop at about 90 minutes.
Five days out: the three close pairs (approve or tell, must or should, function or engagement), then Section A and a short untimed set in your weakest section.
Four days out: one short timed mock. Then recall the final communication, follow-up and escalation, and how the function stays independent.
Three days out: Sections B and C from the chief audit executive's seat, then the principles on planning and on reading the question. No timed tests from today on.
Two days out: light review. Say the priority words and the answering routine from memory, then check. Confirm your appointment, ID and route.
One day out: rest. Glance at your own short list of rules, get ready for the morning, and sleep at your usual time.
items: Nothing new this week. The plan sharpens what you already know; a topic you have never studied is better left alone now.
Missed a day? Skip it and carry on with the next one. Never double up.
Recall beats rereading: answer from memory first, then check.
Practice results in any study app, including KaiSip, are not The IIA's scaled scores and cannot predict your result.

sections.title: Registering and fees
sections.summary: You apply to the CIA program once, register for Part 3, then book a seat at a Pearson VUE test center. The IIA's prices change on 4 January 2027.
steps: Check that you meet the entry rule for the three-part route: a degree, or an active Internal Audit Practitioner (IAP) designation.
Apply to the CIA program and pay the application fee, if you have not already done so for another part. Once you are approved, you have 3 years to complete the program.
Register for Part 3 and pay the exam fee. A registration lasts 180 days, unless your program expires sooner.
Book your appointment at a Pearson VUE test center inside that window.
items: Until 3 January 2027: application fee US$120 for IIA members and US$240 for non-members; Part 3 exam fee US$280 for members and US$415 for non-members.
From 4 January 2027: application fee US$145 for members and US$195 for non-members; Part 3 exam fee US$325 for members and US$435 for non-members.
These are The IIA's listed prices for the United States, Canada and some other countries. Where a national institute of The IIA runs the exams, prices may differ.
Fees are not refunded and cannot be transferred.
Need more time? On the three-part route you can buy one 75-day extension of an exam registration for US$100, and one 12-month extension of the program for US$275.
You can change an appointment up to 48 hours before it. Pearson VUE charges US$75 each time.

sections.title: Test center only
sections.summary: The exam is taken in person, on a computer, at a Pearson VUE test center. The IIA ended online testing on 27 May 2025.
items: There is no at-home or online option. Advice that mentions remote testing for this exam is out of date.
Choose a test center and a time of day that suit you, and book early enough to get both. Your appointment must fall inside your 180-day registration.
You can move the appointment up to 48 hours before it, for a Pearson VUE fee of US$75 each time.
The check-in, ID and test-room rules are for The IIA and Pearson VUE to set. Read them in the current candidate handbook and in your appointment confirmation; KaiSip does not restate them.
Plan the trip ahead: know the route, the travel time and a backup, so nothing about the morning is left to chance.

sections.title: Exam day
sections.summary: Arrive with time in hand, pace by your two checkpoints, and answer every question.
items: Bring what The IIA's candidate handbook and your appointment confirmation tell you to bring. Check the ID rules a few days ahead, while there is still time to fix a problem.
100 questions in 120 minutes. Checkpoints: question 50 by minute 60; question 75 by minute 90.
No breaks are scheduled. If you take one, the clock keeps running.
Answer every question. Wrong answers are not penalized, so a best guess always beats a blank.

For each question: read the last line, decide whether it is about the function or one engagement, find the actor and the priority word, rule out two options, then settle the final two with a principle.
If your mind goes blank, breathe out slowly, pick your best answer for now and return to it if time allows.

sections.title: After the exam
sections.summary: You do not see a score when you finish. The official result arrives within 3 weeks of your exam date.
items: No immediate unofficial score is shown. Official results arrive within 3 weeks of the exam date.
A pass report shows no numeric score. A report for an exam that was not passed shows the score and the syllabus areas that need improvement.
If you did not pass, you can sit again no sooner than 30 days after your last attempt.
An exam may be taken at most eight times during your program eligibility window, and the program's 3-year clock keeps running.
Treat a report that lists areas to improve as a study map: start with the areas it names, then compare them with your KaiSip section percents.
Passing Part 3 is one step. The other parts you still need, and the experience requirement, stand between you and the CIA.

sections.title: Becoming certified
sections.summary: Passing Part 3 does not make you a Certified Internal Auditor. You also pass the other parts and show internal audit experience. The IIA decides every application.
steps: Pass all three parts within 3 years of your program approval, or Parts 2 and 3 if you hold an active Internal Audit Practitioner (IAP) designation. The IIA does not prescribe the order.
Show internal audit experience: 1 year with a master's degree, or 2 years with a bachelor's degree.
Or, as an active IAP holder, show 5 years of experience. An IAP holder who also has a degree needs the 1 or 2 years that go with that degree.
items: You may sit the exams before the experience is complete. The experience is needed to be certified, not to test.
The IIA's CIA page adds that 2 of an IAP holder's 5 years must fall within the past 3 years.
The candidate handbook also lists a route with 5 years of experience and no degree, but the CIA page showed no such route when checked. If you plan to rely on it, confirm with The IIA first.
KaiSip has not checked the rules for keeping the certification once you hold it. Read them on The IIA's site when you get there.
